name: Apple cider vinegar

lead: Apple cider vinegar is made by fermenting apple juice first into alcohol and then into acetic acid. It is a common kitchen ingredient and has a long folk-medicine history. In looksmaxxing forums it is promoted as a cheap all-round ingredient for fat loss, skin, hair and digestion.

Published reviews summarised by Wikipedia and Grokipedia describe limited or poor-quality evidence for weight loss. Small studies have looked at blood glucose and cholesterol with modest results, and the Mayo Clinic is quoted as saying it is unlikely to cause meaningful weight loss.

paras: The active component is generally taken to be acetic acid, about 5 percent of the liquid. Proposed explanations for metabolic effects include slower stomach emptying and effects on post-meal glucose and insulin. Topical claims for acne and dandruff rest on its acidity and in-vitro antimicrobial activity. Which of these mechanisms matter in people has not been established.

Reported problems include tooth enamel erosion, throat or esophageal injury from tablets, reflux and stomach upset, and skin burns or eye injury when used undiluted on the body. Possible interactions with insulin and diuretics are noted. Food amounts are generally regarded as safe by regulators; supplements are not regulated as medicines for weight loss.

lead: Apple cider vinegar (ACV) is a vinegar made from apple juice by two-step fermentation: yeast convert sugars to alcohol, then acetic acid bacteria convert the alcohol to acetic acid. The finished product is roughly 94 percent water and 5 percent acetic acid with almost no fat, protein or micronutrients. Unfiltered versions contain a cloudy cellulose-and-bacteria sediment called the mother. [1][2]

Besides cooking and preserving, ACV is promoted in wellness and looksmaxxing communities as a drink for fat loss and appetite control and as a skin toner, hair rinse and dandruff treatment. Wikipedia states that there is no high-quality clinical evidence that regular consumption helps with weight loss or maintenance, and that major health bodies do not recommend it for therapeutic use. [1] Grokipedia cites the Mayo Clinic as saying it is unlikely to cause meaningful weight loss and cites meta-analyses suggesting modest effects on blood glucose and cholesterol in some trials. [2]
Reported adverse effects include dental enamel damage, esophageal injury from tablets, and gastrointestinal discomfort. [1]
infobox: Food; some topical products carry OTC drug labels

paras: Apples are washed, crushed and pressed; yeast ferment the juice into cider; acetic acid bacteria then oxidise the alcohol to acetic acid, either added as a culture or as mother vinegar. [1] Per 100 g the product is about 94 percent water and 5 percent acetic acid, with roughly 22 kcal. [1]
Commercial brands have been reported to vary in acidity, and some were found contaminated with mould and yeast. [1]

Vinegar of various kinds has been used for thousands of years for preservation, food and folk medicine; Grokipedia traces vinegar-based remedies to ancient Babylon, Egypt and Greece and describes apple vinegar becoming a household staple in Europe and colonial America. [2] Wikipedia notes that fruit vinegars became popular in the North Atlantic region in the early 19th century, citing an 1810 cookbook with apple cider vinegar recipes. [1]
Grokipedia describes a rise in health-food marketing after the Second World War and of raw, unpasteurised varieties promoted for their mother in the 1990s. [2]

Forum users promote diluted ACV as a face toner, spot treatment, hair rinse and scalp treatment, and as a drink for fat loss. [3] A US-labelled over-the-counter scalp spray containing apple cider vinegar is marketed to help with flaking and itching associated with dandruff, with directions for external use only. [4]
ACV is used in cooking, dressings, marinades and pickling. [2] Wellness sources promote it for digestion and blood sugar control. [2]

Wikipedia reports that there is no high-quality clinical evidence of benefit for weight loss or maintenance and no good evidence that it effectively manages blood glucose or lipids. [1] Grokipedia summarises systematic reviews as finding reductions in post-meal glucose and insulin when taken with carbohydrate meals and modest reductions in fasting glucose and HbA1c with use over about eight weeks, while noting that the evidence is limited. [2]

In laboratory work, a 2018 study reported antimicrobial activity of ACV against Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus aureus and Candida albicans in vitro. [5] A 2011 rat study compared apple cider vinegars made with different techniques on blood lipids in animals fed a high-cholesterol diet. [6] Neither study tested skin or weight outcomes in people.

A 2020 systematic review, summarised by Wikipedia, found diluted moderate consumption generally low-risk. Reported harms include esophageal damage from incompletely swallowed tablets, tooth enamel erosion from large amounts, dentin sensitivity, burping, flatulence and more frequent bowel movements. Eye contact may cause corneal injury, and topical use can cause burns. [1]

Wikipedia also lists possible interactions with insulin and diuretics, allergic reactions in people allergic to apples, and a recommendation of caution in pregnancy, breastfeeding and children. [1] Grokipedia adds that concentrated supplements may worsen reflux and delay stomach emptying. [2]

Registered human trials include a comparison of metformin with ACV in people with prediabetes [7], a study of ACV on glycaemic variability and lipids in type 2 diabetes [8], an acute study on an oxidative stress marker after meals in adults with obesity [9], and a study of vinegar and heartburn [10]. Results for these registrations were not available in the listings reviewed. No registered trial listed examines ACV for acne, hair or facial appearance. Meta-analytic findings on glucose and lipids are described above. [2]

On looksmax.org a poster describes ACV as a top ingredient that affects skin, hair, weight, digestion and hormones, listing acne reduction, hair shine and fat burning among its effects. Replies in the thread frame gut health and fermented foods as under-discussed looksmaxxing tools. [3]

lore.intro: ACV is discussed on looksmax.org as a low-cost generalist tool for skin, hair, fat loss and gut health. [3]
